questions.resolution: Resolved 2026-09-06, with a better answer than either option originally posed: Bleed is neither passively visible nor permanently hidden - it is TESTED. A pilot spends a discretionary slice on a Harmonics Evaluation to learn the current value, and that same evaluation can also improve it. Information becomes a purchase in personal time, matching the pattern contactPool.analysisDutyInteraction already set. questions.notes: 2026-09-06 analysis (the retired Resonance and Bleed analysis (deleted 2026-09-25) §3) argues this one is not neutral: Pushing trades Resonance now for Bleed later, and a trade with one side hidden is a gamble rather than a decision. Recommended middle path — show the pilot a BAND (Stable/Strained/Critical) rather than a number: enough to price a push honestly, not enough to count down precisely to berserk, and it matches the three-light-gauge idiom the console already uses. questions.question: Bleed has four defined sources (pushing, Frame damage, plug distress, Suppression) and exactly one undefined reduction (Signals Liaison reduces Bleed, no magnitude or rate given). With no decay, no per-session reset and no downtime route, berserk arrives on a schedule regardless of player choices — a countdown rather than a managed risk. Is that the intent? If not, what are Bleed sinks and at what rates?
questions.resolution: Moot, 2026-09-25 (the cull of stale material). Bleed was cut on 2026-09-20 (bleed-playability), so it needs no recovery sinks. Nothing left to decide.

Episode 1 scripts berserk into the very first fight, which suggests the countdown reading may already be the de facto intent. design/downtime-activities.md proposes one sink (Night Out, -1).

questions.question: config.json bandDesignNote states that most of the campaign is played at 2 actions. SF2E is architecturally a three-action system — two-action activities consume a whole turn, the signature turn shapes need three, and the multiple attack penalty is built around a third attack being possible-but-unwise. Should 3 actions instead be the norm from Nominal upward, with 2 reserved for Dead Weight as a genuine failure state, letting ability tiers and internal-power duration carry the band spread?
questions.resolution: Resolved 2026-09-06: 3 actions is the norm from Nominal upward; 2 actions is a penalty state with exactly two causes, Dead Weight sync and Frame damage (Degraded caps at 2, Critical at 1). User's framing: 'we need to build around the normal being 3 actions and 2 actions being the penalty for early campaign usage and for usage when the mech is seriously damaged.' config.json updated; reasoning preserved in resonance.actionEconomyRevisionNote.
questions.notes: Raised 2026-09-06. The counter-argument is real and artistic: constraint IS the fiction, and Harmonised should feel like a breakthrough. The concern is that a reduced action economy delivers both feels-constrained and has-fewer-decisions, and only the first is wanted.

questions.question: Measured total combat contribution across the Resonance bands (actions per round x internal-power rounds, plus Absolute free Strikes) is 7 / 12 / 24 / 40 actions — a 5.7x spread from Dead Weight to Absolute, before ability tiers are counted. That is a wider gap than four character levels in SF2E, on one track, inside one tier, between players at the same table. Is that intended, and if so should pilots fielded together be constrained to within a band or two of each other?
questions.resolution: Addressed 2026-09-06 by the action-economy change rather than by capping who deploys together. With 3 actions from Nominal, the normal operating range (Nominal to Absolute) compresses from 3.3x to 2.2x. Dead Weight to Absolute remains 5.7x, which is now correct rather than alarming: Dead Weight is explicitly the failure state, and a pilot below 40% sync being a fraction of a working Frame is the intended fiction. The original concern was pilots at 55% being in that position, which no longer happens.
questions.notes: Arithmetic run 2026-09-06; it had not been computed before. Closely tied to two-action-default — making 3 actions standard from Nominal compresses the action-count spread to roughly 2.2x and shifts the difference onto ability tiers, which is arguably where it belongs anyway.

Raised 2026-09-06. Also worth being deliberate about the broader overlap: Hero Points and Anchors both reward selfless or daring play and will often fire on the same moments, at different timescales.

2026-09-24 (LEDGER #31 item 14; Ingram, Casebook D11): no berserk. 'Mitflit technology has no reason to go berserk', and nothing in this campaign takes control of a character away from their player. With Bleed already cut (2026-09-20, bleed-playability), this question has no premise left. It stays open only because closing it is Ingram's call; the recommendation is to close it as moot. questions.question: Frames DO level up (confirmed 2026-09-06; campaign-arc.md had already corrected the design bible on this). The new model: players earn upgrade points from downtime activities AND from winning both personnel- and Frame-scale combat, spend them on Frame upgrades, and enough points levels the Frame — a normal SF2E level-up with bespoke Frame feats and options. Combat awards guarantee a floor so no Frame is ever stranded at 12. Open parameters: what are the points called, what is the points-to-level conversion, are they per-pilot or drawn from a shared pool like technician-days, and what are the concrete DOWNSIDES of over-investing in Frame upgrades at the expense of personal activities?
questions.resolution: RESOLVED 2026-09-20 -- it survives, as a reskinned SF2E equipment economy rather than an abstract points pool. Ingram: "it is essentially a version of SF2E but with a lot of reskinning." Players get a BUDGET. Each Frame gets an initial loadout mirroring the machine's real job and how that tool behaves in combat. Frames carry their own feats, weapons, armour and equipment exactly like a PC: some consumable and renewable, some permanent with once-per-round/hour/day abilities. Worked examples: a Crane Frame plays like a spear with reach, at city scale; a recon vehicle assists Recall Knowledge. Levelling is milestone and lockstep (see levelling-and-request-fulfilment), so upgrade spending buys CAPABILITY, never levels -- which is exactly what dissolves the old contradiction between a points economy and lockstep.
questions.notes: PARTIALLY ANSWERED 2026-09-06. (a) DRIFT: hard cap of one level either way. User: 'rewards players up to a point for investment but doesn't allow there to be an overpowering advantage to just doing frame stuff', and it keeps the encounter maths reliable. This supersedes campaign-arc.md's strict-lockstep line, which is now annotated there. (b) POOL: upgrade points are INDIVIDUAL per pilot, not shared like technician-days — each PC has their own repair crew (see repair-crew-relationship). STILL OPEN: what the points are called, and the points-to-level conversion rate.

questions.question: Downtime activities grant flavoured, predictable buffs — the user's example: 'they only have to go to the gun range once to get a buff which they know will make their next personnel level battle easier by making it easier to hit baddies.' DURATION ANSWERED 2026-09-06: a buff persists until used, and is spent on the character's next combat — bankable, one-shot, not use-it-or-lose-it. STILL OPEN: whether several different buffs can be carried into the same fight, and whether there is a cap.
questions.notes: Useful half-answer already in the system: if activity buffs are expressed as CIRCUMSTANCE bonuses, SF2E's own stacking rules cap them for free — two circumstance bonuses to the same roll don't stack, you take the highest, so hoarding three gun-range visits does nothing. Different bonus TYPES (circumstance + status + item) would all still apply, which is a natural, system-native ceiling rather than an invented one. The remaining risk to watch is a player banking several DIFFERENT-typed buffs ahead of a Contact they can see coming. The design principle is settled even though the parameters are not: buffs must be LEGIBLE and PLANNABLE — a player should be able to predict the payoff before spending the slice. That is the positive twin of ux-doctrine Law 19 (nothing expires without its cost being visible first). Circumstance bonuses are the safest vehicle since they are bounded and native to SF2E, and per design-layers.md this is a Layer 2 addition that must not distort the Layer 0 combat maths underneath.

questions.question: Each pilot has their own repair crew (confirmed 2026-09-06, alongside the decision that upgrade points are individual rather than pooled). The crew is a standing NPC relationship with real mechanical weight in both directions: treat them well — the user's example is going out drinking with them — and they may put in an unasked-for night shift; neglect them and they provide less HP healing per repair. Open parameters: how is crew standing tracked, what exactly does it scale (HP restored per technician-day? chance of free work? both?), how many named crew NPCs per pilot, and how does crew standing interact with the SHARED technician-day pool?
questions.notes: PARTIALLY ANSWERED 2026-09-09. (a) NAMED NPCS: one per pilot, six total, confirmed and scaffolded as placeholders (data/npcs/repair-chief-*.json, linked via npc.schema.json's new crewChiefForRef) — currently 'lesser NPCs who may grow into bigger more interesting roles later,' not characterised yet. (b) WHAT IT SCALES: a guaranteed baseline HP repair happens every technician-day cycle regardless of PC involvement (the floor — 'repair crews are always working around the clock'); direct PC involvement, working alongside the crew rather than just spending the resource, restores substantially more. STILL OPEN, numeric: the exact floor amount and the exact PC-involvement multiplier/bonus are not set. (c) VEHICLES: confirmed the same crew also maintains the pilot's assigned chassis (campaign/chassis-catalogue.json, added 2026-09-09) from the same technician-day allocation, so splitting a limited pool between a Frame and a vehicle is a real player choice — this wasn't a live question when the entry was first written, since vehicles as a concrete catalogue didn't exist yet. The two resources are still cleanly non-redundant: the technician-day pool is the Directorate's SHARED allocation — how much repair time you are granted, competed for between pilots — while crew standing/involvement is PERSONAL and scales how much you get OUT of that time. This also gives the Night Out rest activity (design/downtime-activities.md §2) a second payoff beyond Bleed reduction, and gives every pilot a recurring named NPC relationship that is professional rather than personal, sitting alongside Anchors rather than duplicating them. TERMINOLOGY WARNING unchanged: these are NPC repair technicians, verbally distinct from the PC-played Ground Roles in the cut ground-roles file (deleted 2026-09-25) (Sensor Operator, Umbilical Control, etc.), which are something else entirely.

questions.question: The Day 1 pilot's stated disadvantage is a real injury that 'permanently lose[s] one discretionary slice per day to ongoing medical obligations' (design-bible.md). That was half their daily options under the original 2-slice economy. The slice count changed to 4 on 2026-09-06 (see timeEconomy.slicesRevisionNote), which quietly halves the real weight of that penalty to a quarter of their options, as a side effect of a UI-driven number that had nothing to do with this character beat when it was decided. Should the loss scale to two slices to preserve the original bite, or is the softer version actually fine or even an improvement?
questions.resolution: Resolved 2026-09-06, and not by rescaling the number. Per the new standing design principle 'penalties cost risk, never choice' (design/campaign-arc.md), a permanent slice loss was always the wrong shape regardless of size. Superseded: the Day 1 pilot's injury is now reduced starting Hit Points at personnel scale, not a discretionary-slice tax. Costs nothing in a Frame (full Resonance, full actions, full slice choice); everything the moment they are not in one, since scale-and-chassis.md §11 already puts a dismounted pilot on foot at personnel scale where Ground Role danger deals real damage against a real HP pool. Their existing advantage (68% starting Resonance) is untouched.
questions.notes: Found during a 2026-09-06 audit pass, not raised at the time the slice count changed — a real example of why cross-file consequences need checking after a number changes, not just the file the number lives in.

questions.question: The Day 1 pilot's injury is now reduced starting Hit Points at personnel scale (resolved 2026-09-06, see day1-pilot-slice-penalty-scaling). The shape is decided; the number is not — how much HP, and is it a flat reduction, a percentage, or a specific ability-score/class-feature change?
questions.notes: Deliberately not invented here — this is a real balance number for a specific named character beat, not something to guess at. Confirmed 2026-09-10 (LEDGER.md #10): this is a player-CHOSEN chargen option ("the Day 1 pilot"/"veteran" start), not an assigned narrative role, and the pilot also starts exhausted from their duties on top of the reduced HP — a plausible fit for the Exhaustion track (design/downtime-activities.md §1, itself still a proposal). The induction terminal has no branch for this path yet; still needs this number before that branch can be built.

questions.question: Does a Directorate records search on day one find Manako, and under what name? dossier-cicada.json section 5 says he appears in every document as a terrorist, which - if true and searchable by trainees - lets a curious party shortcut the entire campaign in Episode One, the same afternoon they meet him.
questions.resolution: Resolved 2026-09-13 (LEDGER #17), option (a) and then strengthened. THE DIRECTORATE HAS NEVER IDENTIFIED CICADA'S FOUNDER. They have a cult, demonstrations, arrests and a cabinet of detained believers, and no name at the top. A day-one search on the old man returns a chemist disgraced decades ago and nothing else, because that is genuinely all the institution has - not because the file is restricted. His name is therefore SAFE to give the table freely, and should be, since the later recognition depends on it having been in their notes all along. Ingram then went further and made it a standing rule: 'the rule should be that it is the player characters who must first identify that The Original Cultist is a key figure in the organisation and they must be the ones to find out it's the kindly man they met during the first session.' Both halves of that discovery belong to the players. No NPC hands them either one. REFINED 2026-09-24 (LEDGER #34): the cult is largely peaceful and largely a non-issue for the Directorate until the adventure properly starts. It has a bit of information about it, not enough to dismantle it, understand its aims, or know the Watcher is active alongside it; the 'cabinet of detained believers' above overstates it. It may know Manako as the scientist it employed and disgraced, and may even suspect he runs the tea house, which salves its conscience; it has no link between him and the cult. The rule stands: both halves of the discovery belong to the players.
questions.notes: Raised 2026-09-13 while writing The Errand, the Episode One scene where the party meets him. The four-pass reveal is designed so his name turns up later in a discredited paper and is ALREADY FAMILIAR, which is the gut-punch - that only works if a day-one search returns nothing useful. Three ways out, not chosen here: (a) the Directorate has never identified Cicada's founder at all, and 'appears as a terrorist' describes the movement rather than the man; (b) he is on file under the name he was disgraced under, which is not the name the tea house knows him by; (c) the file exists and trainees have no access to it on day one, which is true of almost everything else they will want. Option (a) is the cleanest and has knock-on effects for what the Directorate knows in later chapters, so it is Ingram's call rather than a detail to settle in a scene brief.

questions.question: Do the five ground roles survive at all, and if so in what form? Raised by Ingram 2026-09-13: 'Umbilical Control as an idea sounds like a player not getting involved and having fun, ground-roles may need completely removing or at least realigning with a SF2E campaign's need to give each player agency over their role and actions.'
questions.resolution: CUT 2026-09-20. Ingram: "Remove this concept. Every player is either in a Frame or a Vehicle for those large scale combats. We might have a student caught with neither but that would only happen under very unusual story circumstances." The five ground roles are gone. Lockstep removed the asymmetry that created them -- six pilots each in their own machine means no non-piloting kid is standing on a Frame-scale battlefield needing a job. Personnel-scale combat still exists in its own right (Episode One is entirely personnel scale); what is cut is a student having a ROLE on the Frame-scale battlefield without a machine. the cut ground-roles file (deleted 2026-09-25) is marked CUT rather than deleted, and roughly 74 files still mention ground roles -- a cleanup sweep is outstanding.
questions.notes:
Three separate problems, worth keeping distinct. (1) AGENCY: Umbilical Control converts a kid's successful check into a resource for somebody else's Frame, and Signals Liaison spends a turn adjusting another player's track - both are a player taking an action whose entire payoff lands on a different player's sheet. That is the specific complaint. (2) DEPENDENCY: two of the five (Umbilical Control, Signals Liaison) only exist when a Frame is on the field, so a player who picks one has a job that cannot come up in a personnel-scale session at all. (3) REACH: 'ground role' appears across 84 files as of 2026-09-13, including the kid schema, the equipment catalogue, the six draft kids, the induction prompts, the battle simulator's whole ground-layer and its six kid fixtures, and data/subsystems/day-1-ground-layer.json. Removing them is not a delete, it is a project. Nothing has been removed; the concept is flagged only. THE STANDING REQUIREMENT, from the same message: this is a heavily modified SF2E campaign first, so every player must have real agency over their own role and actions, and no design should stray from what makes a good SF2E table experience.

GOVERNING PRINCIPLE ADDED 2026-09-19, from a real played example rather than an abstract preference: "Something that DID NOT work well for me in SF1E was the spaceship combat, multiple players controlling or working through a single thing/token/machine actually sucks in real life because players get less ability to express themselves." This sharpens problem (1) above into a hard rule for whatever ground roles become: no design may route several players' turns into one shared token/machine's payoff. Tied to frame-scale-starting-level and resonance-playability/bleed-playability under issue #194 -- if that question resolves toward lockstep+reflavour (six pilots, each in their own same-level Frame, rather than one pilot plus five ground-support kids), the shared-token problem may dissolve on its own rather than needing a ground-role redesign to solve it directly.

questions.question: Resonance needs substantial work before it is functional, interesting or playable. What does it actually become? Flagged by Ingram 2026-09-13 alongside Bleed.
questions.resolution: CUT 2026-09-20. Ingram, asked whether to rework or cut: "Cut these concepts for now." Resonance is removed from the design; it is not being reworked and nothing should be built on it. the retired Resonance and Bleed analysis (deleted 2026-09-25) is kept because it remains the DIAGNOSIS of why it did not work, not because the system is live. FOLLOW-ON, NOT YET DECIDED: Anchors (config.json#anchors) existed primarily as the GM lever on Resonance, and Suppression (config.json#suppression) existed solely to close a Resonance exploit. Neither has been ruled on -- see anchors-without-resonance.
questions.notes:
Supersedes the previous framing in which Resonance was treated as locked and authoritative (CLAUDE.md carried that claim until 2026-09-13, when it was corrected). The original question (level 4 instead of level 12) was Ingram's own opening move; her fuller answer, asked again the same day, supersedes it: "The whole idea of mechs being level 4 and players starting at level 1 needs rethinking. Maybe what we need is simpler and better, mechs and pilots stay in lock step, we reflavour everything for mechs so that players can feel like their abilities are unique or unusual and this way we keep the ability for characters to still have an effect on the big battlefield." This is a candidate to replace the retired two-scale design (deleted 2026-09-25)'s entire premise (two hard-separated scales, three legal interfaces, a level-1 kid and a level-12 Frame as separate character sheets) with one character, one level, reflavoured for Frame scale rather than built twice. questions.resolution: RESOLVED 2026-09-20. Lockstep, not hard-separated: pilot and Frame share one level, full stop. Frame combat begins within the party's first two levels -- utility Frames adapted into combat use through play, never handed a combat-purpose mech outright -- and the party is 'solidly combat mech pilots' by level 3. Gen 2 access stays a long way off past that (see gen2-tradeoff-mechanism, resolved the same day). The Watcher and Cicada both keep probing/escalating the city in the meantime, which is what supplies an encounter-appropriate threat at every step rather than ever putting a level-1 party in front of a level-12 Claimant -- and it dissolves this question's original motivating problem for free: dossier-observer.md §8 already established Claimant mass 'ranges from insect to behemoth,' so a small, weak, early Claimant for a small, weak, early party was always legal, it just hadn't been said aloud. the retired two-scale design (deleted 2026-09-25)'s own banner is updated to match. Players are not told why any of this is happening -- see the DNA-reveal timing note on gen2-tradeoff-mechanism.

questions.question: What actually makes an early second-generation Frame 'worse in some ways' than a heavily-upgraded first-generation one, mechanically?
questions.notes: Raised 2026-09-19 (LEDGER #21), Ingram's own words: "those mechs will initially be worse in some ways than people who instead opt to continue upgrading their lower tech mechs instead... just in case people become really attached to their mechs in their original forms." dossier-second-generation-frames.md §7 guessed the simplest mechanism -- switching largely restarts the Frame's own upgrade-point investment -- but flagged it as a guess, not a decision. That guess is superseded by the actual answer below.
questions.resolution: RESOLVED 2026-09-20. An inherent compatibility/instability mechanic, not an upgrade-investment opportunity cost: switching into an unsynced Gen 2 Frame costs Slowed 1 until synced. Grounded in a real precedent -- even Anabala, the one founder who could fly a Gen 2 prototype at all, suffered this same sync problem (dossier-second-generation-frames.md §3, updated same day). That's exactly why swapping Gen 2 Frames on a whim is a real bad idea rather than a strictly-better upgrade, and it's an inherent property of the pilot/machine bond rather than anything the upgrade-point economy needs to change. Players don't learn any of this -- or their own DNA marker -- until roughly level 4, at first Gen 2 contact; Episode One and Two plant nothing early. The exact sync-clearing mechanism (how long, what activity, whether it fades with use) is not decided -- see gen2-sync-duration-mechanism.

questions.question: Once a pilot takes Slowed 1 for switching into an unsynced Gen 2 Frame, what actually clears it -- a fixed downtime cost (a real named activity, like the existing rest/sync-training roster), something that fades naturally with continued use in play, a one-time tax that never recurs once bonded, or something else?
questions.notes: Spun off 2026-09-20 from gen2-tradeoff-mechanism the moment Ingram confirmed the mechanism itself (Slowed 1 on an unsynced Gen 2 Frame, grounded in Anabala's own precedent) -- resolved the same conversation, minutes later.
questions.resolution: RESOLVED 2026-09-20. Named 'Frame Sickness' -- a well-known, in-fiction phenomenon pilots are warned about in advance, not a hidden gotcha. Slowed 1 for the ENTIRE first fight in a given Gen 2 Frame; gone from the second fight in that same Frame onward. Ingram's own words: "being slowed one for a whole fight is already a very brutal penalty to operate under." Read as per-Frame, not a one-time character tax: climbing into a DIFFERENT Gen 2 unit re-triggers it, which is exactly why swapping between Gen 2 Frames on a whim stays a bad idea even after a pilot has fully synced with one of them -- flag for confirmation when this is actually built, since it was inferred from phrasing rather than stated in those exact terms. CONFIRMED AND EXTENDED 2026-09-20: per-machine is correct, and the reasoning is explicit -- 'we don't want players swapping mechs every single session or hoping from a broken mech into a working one without fixing the broken one.' Ingram's own comparison is PF2E magic item investment, though more substantive. It is a ONE-TIME penalty per machine, players are told exactly what to expect in advance, and an early Gen 2 TRAINING EXERCISE is to be built specifically so the party can burn through Frame Sickness safely rather than eating it in a real fight. HIDDEN FROM PLAYERS, GM-ONLY: sticking with the same Gen 2 Frame pays off quietly -- a small bonus around the 5th session with it, another small boost around the 9th combat. Players are never told these exist; loyalty is rewarded, not advertised.

questions.question: Do Frames and vehicles use SF2E's own vehicle rules, or something else?
questions.notes: Ingram ran her own deep-dive on SF2E's vehicle rules 2026-09-20 and came back with a decision the same day.
questions.resolution: RESOLVED 2026-09-20. NOT the SF2E vehicle system -- Ingram: 'it's not really suitable and adds far too many complications to the way that vehicles move to be helpful.' Instead both Frames and vehicles get their own PC-grade character sheets (real statblocks), and Foundry gets a way to associate pilot and machine so they move together, with buttons to reach both sheets or swap between them at a press. At level 1 Frames and vehicles are deliberately basic: they contribute HARDNESS and HIGH AC (the things that make Frame-scale combat survivable) and they amplify the pilot's own sheet rather than replacing it -- a spellcaster's magic reaching across huge distances is the worked example. The effect is a reskin of the PC's own character sheet from personnel scale to Frame scale, changing as little about how SF2E works as possible. Frames: very slow, very tough, high AC, high saves, real hardness. Vehicles: some extremely fast, but fragile -- destroyed means the pilot ejects, takes damage, and is in a much worse position. Even the smallest vehicle carries up to three passengers, which makes vehicles the party's way to move students and evacuate downed pilots. THREE equally important tracks, not a hierarchy: student pilots (near-raw personnel-scale SF2E), Frames, and vehicles. Every player gets the choice of a Frame; a player may spend the whole campaign never using one, or never using a vehicle, and both are fine. When Gen 2 tech arrives, Gen 1 vehicles need equivalent upgrades so that track stays live.

questions.question: What does the party's first Frame-scale enemy encounter actually consist of, now that no Claimant stat block exists in the project at all?

All three are PROTO-Claimants -- at this point the Watcher does not have a clear idea of what it is doing or how to do it effectively, which is what licenses them being strange and inefficient rather than optimised. Build it as a deliberately hard encounter by real XP budget, select three interesting creatures from the existing SF2E library, and reskin them in Foundry so descriptions and information fit the brief -- do not stat three new creatures from scratch. NAMING CONVENTION, new and reusable: enemies at world-map scale get a military contact designation, the way a radar or sonar operator designates an unknown contact -- letters and numbers carrying some basic information while explicitly admitting the target is unidentified. Those designations come off the plotting floor (data/locations/the-plot-room.json) and are read to the party over the radio by comms-officer.json.

questions.question: Why does the Observer start probing the city's defences when it does -- tied to Manako's own arc, or a separate, more independent escalation?
questions.notes:
Raised 2026-09-19 (LEDGER #21). This is the trigger that forces the Directorate to deploy whatever Frames are ready (including the party's utility ones), pulling them into real Frame combat for the first time -- the concrete cause behind the already-agreed Episode Two shape (ch1-v2.md §8). Left deliberately open whether it's caused by / tied to dossier-cicada.md §13.1's five movements or is its own thread.

2026-09-24 (LEDGER #31) -- a note, not a resolution; still open. #31 recasts the Watcher: it is the generation ship's navigation and sensor system and the campaign's adversary, with the objective to multiply, to expand and to keep observing, and it learns how to defeat the party if they get in its way (item 4). Two things now bear on this. (1) Its children are given purposes of their own, and the runaway begins when those children start producing their own Sap (item 8; Ingram, D4: 'The Watcher learns'). Read one way, the probing is the start of that same escalation (a reading, not a decision). (2) A mass-gated PROPOSAL, Claude's, in the Casebook and in ideas/story/dossier-observer.md's section on its children, would answer this: at first it can condense only where Sap has been released, so every early attack carries a cult fingerprint; later it is dense enough to condense wherever attention pools, with no Sap at all. Not decided. One wording clash to settle if it is adopted: the proposal calls its Chapters 5-10 stage 'the probing', while LEDGER #21 and ideas/story/dossier-second-generation-frames.md §5a use 'probing' for what first pulls the party into Frame combat within the first two levels. Under the proposal, those early call-outs are condensations at Sap-release sites.

2026-09-27 (LEDGER #40) -- bears on this; still open. The Watcher 'observes, adapts and responds' and escalates without understanding why; so long without a guiding framework, it has drifted from helpful to an accidental antagonist. Its escalation ends in a weapon built from exotic matter (Second Impact). Nobody knows it exists until the party uncovers it.

2026-09-27 (LEDGER #41) -- bears on this; still open. After Second Impact the Watcher stays over Kurose as a perpetual threat: nothing has stopped its escalation, so it goes on causing chaos and probing the city's defences, without malice.

questions.question: What is the Section Officer's actual name?
questions.label: The Section Officer
questions.notes: MERGED FROM naming-placeholders.json, 2026-09-19. Original description: "The party's immediate superior and the campaign's in-house petty tyrant (data/npcs/section-officer.json). Needs a name that sounds like a middling rank on a duty roster rather than a villain -- the joke is that he is completely ordinary. Whatever it is, the party will say it a great deal, usually while complaining."
questions.resolution:
RESOLVED by Ingram, 2026-09-21: "Give the Section Officer a name - That really should have been done a long time ago." Named VETCH, surname only.

WHY IT FITS THE BRIEF. The question asked for a name that sounds like a middling rank on a duty roster rather than a villain, because the joke is that he is completely ordinary. Vetch is a fodder crop -- a real, dull, slightly unpleasant English surname with nothing grand about it. It is also built to be said a great deal while complaining: one syllable, hard final consonant, and it snaps.

WHY SURNAME ONLY. The bible's own naming doctrine, quoted in prose-craft-and-naming.md section 11: given names for the young and the outsiders, surnames for the institution. He is the institution. It also rhymes with his single most characteristic habit -- he calls the party Section Nine and never by name, and nobody uses his given name either, including him.

PHONETIC CLEARANCE. Checked against every named NPC (Hulda Brack, Shucks Mordant, Nobu, Taka, Manako) under the first-stressed-syllable rule rather than the first-letter rule. No V name exists anywhere in the cast, so the lane is completely clear, and the nearest institutional surname in register -- Brack -- shares neither onset, vowel nor coda.

questions.question: Does the Flood Tunnel Clearance encounter award 80 XP or 120 XP?
questions.label: Flood Tunnel Clearance XP award
questions.notes: Found 2026-09-19 during the overnight fragmentation sweep (a background agent auditing data/encounters/ for drift against ch1-v2.md). data/encounters/c1e1-flood-tunnel.json currently awards a flat 120 XP, citing ch1-v2.md's "Moderate, 120" label as its source. But that label in ch1-v2.md §6 is explicitly the encounter's BUILD size (how many Centipedes are on the map), not its award -- ch1-v2.md §1's own ledger table separately lists this encounter's AWARD as 80, under a stated rule: "Build bigger, award the same" (the encounter is built at six-PC scale for a real fight, but XP awards stay pinned to the four-player baseline value so leveling pace doesn't silently double). Both readings are internally consistent within their own section; they simply disagree with each other, and nobody has reconciled them. This is the first real XP award of the campaign and sets the leveling-pace precedent for everything after it, so the number matters more than its size suggests.

questions.question: The gods told Rupiah the next rift would open in Kurose "many hundreds of years in the future" — but the present day is about two hundred years after Kortos. Is the rift due now, still centuries off, or genuinely unknowable?
questions.label: When the foretold rift is due
questions.notes: Raised 2026-09-24 while recording the founding prophecy (ideas/story/bible/LEDGER.md #25, dossier-first-impact.md §10a). Ingram also said the threat "cannot be precisely predicted in time", so one answer is that nobody — not even the founders — knows.
questions.resolution: Resolved 2026-09-24 (Ingram): nobody knows, because the conditions are not yet right — which is why augury and fortune-telling magic return no answer. The players and the antagonists will bring the right mix of things together, about three-quarters of the way through the campaign, and the second rift is then unstoppable from here: the party must take a spaceship to the mitflit home world to bring back the means to stop the exotic-matter runaway, and the last quarter is a starship campaign with the players as command staff on an enterprise-sized intergalactic ship. The cause is deliberately open (a cultist detonating stolen mitflit ship fuel on purpose, an accident, or a tragic misunderstanding). GM-ONLY: 'don't tell the players too much'. See design/campaign-arc.md and ideas/story/bible/LEDGER.md #26. SUPERSEDED 2026-09-27 (LEDGER #40): the cause is a weapon the Watcher builds from exotic matter, without understanding what it can do.

questions.question: The older account had the Directorate follow a trail from the crater to the rest of the ship's hull under Kurose. The prophecy now replaces that as the reason they came. Is the hull still under Kurose — and is it what the gods foresaw?
questions.label: Is the hull under Kurose?
questions.notes:
Raised 2026-09-24. The hull under the city carries later plot weight in the v4 bible (§5: the hull is under the city; Chapter Eight is a voyage). dossier-first-impact.md §7 is marked superseded in part until this is answered.

2026-09-24 (LEDGER #31 item 1): the hull under Kurose belongs to a SECOND ship, the search ship that came a thousand years after the generation ship to find out what had happened to it -- not the rest of the ship that fell at Kortos. The resolution below still holds: the hull is under Kurose, and it is why the gods named Kurose.

2026-09-27 (LEDGER #42): the city sits on the first dig, which found the hull; the second excavation, which reaches the whole ship, is a journey from the city, off the city map.
questions.resolution: Resolved 2026-09-24 (Ingram): yes — the hull is under Kurose, and it is WHY the gods foresaw the rift there. The Directorate came for the prophecy and later found what it was sitting on, so the older trail-to-the-hull account and the new prophecy both hold. LEDGER #26.

Reconciled the same day by Claude under Ingram's standing permission to fill blanks (LEDGER #27, open to veto) as 'famous names, sanitised faces': the city knows the four by name, but every approved picture shows four tall humans and the approved history never says how the rift opened. questions.question: What is the machine found buried impossibly deep in the Kortos crater -- the bisected specimen every Gen 1 Frame is copied from? Ingram's working assumption is a teleportation accident: the machine ended up inside the rock itself and could never be extracted. To decide: whose machine it is (part of the generation ship, something from the search ship, or neither), how and when it came to be inside the rock, and how that sits with the existing account that the rift bisected it on the way down.
questions.notes:
Raised 2026-09-24 from Ingram's correction A3.2, filed as LEDGER #31 item 23 and flagged there as needing clarification: "I assume that the machine that was buried deep was the result of a teleportation accident, ending up within the rock itself and impossible to extract. This is an area we should flag as being in need of clarification." The existing account (ideas/story/dossier-first-impact.md): a specimen buried 'far deeper than should have been possible -- deeper than dwarven caverns', bisected by the aperture, whose cross-section let the era's magic-users reverse-engineer the Frames. It matters more now that there are two ships (LEDGER #31 item 1): Gen 1 is copied from this specimen, Gen 2 is built from the search ship under Kurose (ideas/story/dossier-second-generation-frames.md), and what the living core inside every Frame is has been re-asked separately as Casebook D13. Nothing here is decided; don't build on any reading.

2026-09-24 (LEDGER #32 item 6): withdrawn; see resolution. Not to be confused with the generation ship's shuttle, which #32 also puts 'buried deep under the rock of Kortos'. The shuttle is a real object, tracked as kortos-shuttle.
questions.resolution: Withdrawn 2026-09-24 (Ingram, Casebook N4; LEDGER #32 item 6): there is no bisected specimen. "We could make this simpler and I think it works just as well. It's not a bisected mech that get's revealed, it's the inner layers of the spaceship (the generation ship) which get's opened up by the rupture." Scientists and magic-users descended on the opened ship, adventurers came for valuables, and the organisations around Kortos banded together to guard it, which is how the Directorate was born. Gen 1 Frames are Golarion technology only, informed by looking at the ship's technology (item 7), so nothing is copied from a single machine, and the teleportation-accident assumption (A3.2, LEDGER #31 item 23) has nothing left to explain. Carried into ideas/story/dossier-second-generation-frames.md (§2, §5b, §8) and ideas/story/bible/species/mitflits.md; ideas/story/dossier-first-impact.md was rewritten to match the same day.

questions.question: Was Mother -- the old campaign's level-15 incorporeal construct, met in the mitflit village and on the generation ship's cargo deck -- the generation ship's reasoning core, the mind the Watcher's reports went to? Claude has proposed yes. Either way: where is she now, in what state, and does she matter to the Watcher or to solving it?
questions.notes:
Raised 2026-09-24 (LEDGER #31). CANON underneath it: the Watcher is the generation ship's navigation and sensor system (item 3). THE PROPOSAL (Claude's fill-in, veto freely): Mother was the ship's reasoning core -- the old ship map has an 'AI Reasoning Core' chamber on its bridge deck -- and First Impact tore the navigation and sensor system away from her, which is the organising layer the swarm lost. LEDGER #31 lists 'Mother's fate' as still open. Source material, not canon: ideas/story/source-material/the-trouble-with-mitflits/campaign-timeline.md (Arc 5: Mother built 8 Nov 2023 at level 15, a construct, incorporeal and highly intelligent) and ideas/story/source-material/BRIEFING-for-an-LLM.md §8, which first asked whether Mother is the ship's AI. ideas/story/dossier-observer.md carries the proposal and points here. Its museum piece, a coherent fragment of the navigation and sensor system that 'possibly' remembers what it answered to, is the nearest existing hook.

2026-09-24 (LEDGER #32 item 3; Ingram, Casebook N1) -- a working answer, not a resolution; still open. "She could still be alive, perhaps in the fragment in the museum? Weakened, unable to control The Watcher directly, but still a valuable witness and source of information for the players." So, as Ingram's own 'perhaps': alive, in the museum fragment; weakened; unable to control the Watcher directly; and a witness and source of information the players can reach. Her answer takes the proposal above (Mother as the ship's mind) as its starting point without objecting to it. LEDGER #32 keeps open 'Mother's fate, if the museum isn't it'. Reconciled the same day: ideas/story/dossier-observer.md first described the museum piece as a fragment of the navigation and sensor system (the Watcher's own layer), and now calls it a fragment of the generation ship, with Mother perhaps alive in it.

2026-09-24 (LEDGER #34, Casebook D13): Ingram's "maybe" that a small part of Mother is in every Gen 2 Frame, as the cerebral glue that makes the technology work. Tracked separately at mother-in-gen2.

2026-09-27 (LEDGER #41): "The fragment of Mother" -- the museum fragment is hers. With the search ship itself, it is the only proof the party has, on the home world, that they represent the descendants of the generation ship's crew. The Watcher's final fate is left open (perhaps permanently dispersed, perhaps surviving and becoming harmless, perhaps scooped out of the air by returning mitflits and taken home), to be built as the ending approaches.

questions.question: Why did the mitflits living by the generation ship, in the hidden jungle valley on Kortos, want its exotic fuel -- the errand during which the four founders caused First Impact? What were they going to do with it, and did they know how dangerous it was?
questions.notes:
Raised 2026-09-24. LEDGER #31 item 22 settles the errand -- First Impact happened while the four were trying to get exotic fuel for the mitflits who lived there (Ingram, A3.1: 'they cause The First Impact when trying to get the exotic fuel for the Mitflits who live there') -- and lists why they wanted it as still open. Related canon: the exotic matter is fuel, and a breached container causes a subspace rupture (item 7); the mitflits are gathering in Kurose so that they can all leave to go home together (ideas/story/bible/species/mitflits.md); the campaign's last quarter needs the home world (LEDGER #26). The obvious reading, fuel to fly home, has not been said by anyone, so don't build on it. Source material: the old campaign's jungle and cargo-deck arcs, including the ship's two reactors and the mitflit village beside it (ideas/story/source-material/the-trouble-with-mitflits/campaign-timeline.md, Arcs 5 and 6).

2026-09-24 (LEDGER #32 item 5): answered; see resolution. The caution above still applies one step on: 'fuel for the shuttle' has been said, but what the shuttle was for (flying home, going for help, anything else) has not.
questions.resolution: Resolved 2026-09-24 (Ingram, Casebook N3; LEDGER #32 item 5), as her own working assumption: the fuel was for the shuttle. "I cannot remember the original reasoning, so let's assume that it was fuel for the Shuttle. The players never got to the shuttle which was buried deep under the rock of Kortos away from the original destroyed spaceship. We can leave this as something that we need to tie up eventually." The shuttle itself, and the rest of what this question asked (what the jungle mitflits meant to do with it, and whether they knew how dangerous the fuel was), is tracked as kortos-shuttle.

questions.question: Why do spaceships fall on Golarion? Ingram's working hypothesis, marked 'perhaps': something about Golarion is both attractive to the mitflits and critically dangerous to exploring ships -- perhaps the gods, jealous of their domain, who foresaw that mitflits landing and spreading freely would change the world in ways they did not want. Is it the gods? If so, which gods, how do they bring ships down, and does anyone in the campaign ever learn it?
questions.notes: Raised 2026-09-24 from Casebook D1, verbatim in LEDGER #31 and summarised there as item 2. Ingram: 'Mitflits aren't evil, they are not a conquering empire, but perhaps Mitflits had identified the world as a potential place to live without understanding the concept of gods and perhaps without even understanding the concept of a territorial domain.' Both ships fell: the generation ship, and the search ship sent after it a thousand years later (item 1). A working hypothesis, not a lock. Things to check it against when it is decided, none of them decided: the gods named Kurose as the place of the next rift (LEDGER #25 and #26), and the search ship's hull lies under Kurose; the old campaign's never-played 'ancient alien god' map (ideas/story/source-material/the-trouble-with-mitflits/campaign-timeline.md §7); and the late-campaign 'something worse beyond' reserve in ideas/entries/antagonist-structure-cicada-org-moral-complexity.json, which this could fill.

questions.question: Where does the old campaign's 'Kortos Cataclysm' fit in Blank Inheritance, if anywhere? In the original campaign's lore it was an Inicrium explosion about a thousand years before 4721 AR (the founders' era, so roughly twelve hundred years before the present day) that left part of Kortos uninhabitable. It is a different event from both the Baldwin Manor battery and First Impact. Keep it as its own old disaster, connect it to something already in the lore, or drop it?
questions.notes: Raised 2026-09-24 (LEDGER #29 left it unplaced; LEDGER #31 lists it as still open). Source: ideas/story/source-material/the-trouble-with-mitflits/journals/inicrium.md, the GM's in-world treatise. Inicrium is 'solid magic potential', a magical battery material that collapses into an unstable grey ball above about 50 g and explodes at around 100 g. Beware a coincidence of numbers: the search ship came 'a thousand years' after the generation ship, but that was tens of thousands of years ago, while the Cataclysm is a thousand years before the founders' era. They are not the same span. The same LEDGER line also leaves two other old-campaign items unplaced, not yet tracked as questions of their own: the never-played 'ancient alien god' map and 'Te'Alay' (campaign-timeline.md in the same folder).

questions.question: What became of the mitflits the old campaign left besieged at Gauntlight Keep? The battle was prepared and never played: 49 mitflits and their royal guard against William Charles Baldwin's army of hunters, infantry, archers and mobs, while the four founders were flung across the planes to Nirvana. Did the mitflits hold, and does the answer reach the present day -- how mitflits remember the four, Anabala, the Baldwin line?
questions.notes: Raised 2026-09-24 (LEDGER #31, 'Still open'). Source: ideas/story/source-material/the-trouble-with-mitflits/campaign-timeline.md §7. The 'Gauntlight Revived' map was set with 49 mitflits, six Royal Guards, Miriq, Esther Williams and Arun against Baldwin's forces, and the mitflits' plea from the cargo deck asked the four to come back through a counterpart portal 'before anyone else gets killed'. Only the GM ever looked at that map. Blank Inheritance exists partly to give that campaign closure (LEDGER #30), and the lord is canon as William Charles Baldwin (LEDGER #31 item 21), so this is one of the loose ends the closure has to answer or deliberately leave. Related: baldwin-line-in-kurose.

questions.question: Baldwin's line in the present day is decided as a beat the players will eventually come across (LEDGER #31 item 24), and LEDGER #32 makes it William Charles Baldwin himself: alive, secret until the right moment, and a criminal lord. What shape does his presence in Kurose take (his organisation, his gangs, his mitflit workshops, any front), and do any descendants exist too?
questions.notes:
Decided as a beat 2026-09-24; its shape is open. Ingram, on Claude's proposal: 'I love the idea of bringing in Baldwin's ancestors and making that a beat the players will eventually come across. That's great.' LEDGER #31 reads 'ancestors' there as his present-day line. CLAUDE'S PROPOSAL, not decided: Baldwin House as the arms concern, or the crime lords, that Manako works with, carrying a two-hundred-year grudge against the four. Background: WCB led the old campaign's mitflit hunters, and when members of his own family died by accident in the shadow siege at Baldwin Manor he blamed the four anyway (item 22). In the source material the Baldwins also ran one of Kortos's largest magical-weapons manufactories (ideas/story/source-material/the-trouble-with-mitflits/journals/history-of-baldwin-manor.md); LEDGER #29 left open whether that carries over.

QUESTION REWORDED 2026-09-24 (LEDGER #32 item 1; Ingram's Baldwin paragraph, and Casebook N9, 'See above'). It used to ask only about his descendants two hundred years on. Now canon, GM-only and secret until the right moment: William Charles Baldwin is alive ("He was insanely rich, that might give him access to ways to stay alive"), a criminal lord who arms criminal gangs with incredible weapons, and those weapons are still made by essentially enslaved mitflits. The four founders are his natural enemies, and meeting him is personal for the players, four of whom played the four. Descendants may exist too; the man matters more (LEDGER #32). CLAUDE'S PROPOSALS (LEDGER #32, veto freely): he is the crime lord Manako works for, at arm's length, so Nobu's laundering, the Fixer's 'crime partners' and the heist crews all run through his organisation; the mitflits gathering in Kurose to go home are easy prey for his workshops; his front might trade under the old castle's name, Croglang. These take over from the earlier proposal above (Baldwin House as the arms concern, or the crime lords Manako works with). Split out the same day: how he stays alive (baldwin-longevity) and when and how he is revealed (baldwin-reveal). His file: ideas/story/bible/characters/william-charles-baldwin.md.

questions.question: The 'berserk protocol' recited at assembly (Mystery Ledger #8, 'the protocol's line about brothers') no longer has a berserk to be about: nothing in this campaign goes berserk (LEDGER #31 item 14). Rework it or cut it? questions.notes:
Raised 2026-09-24 (LEDGER #31, Claude's fill-in, veto freely). Where it still appears as 'the berserk protocol': ideas/story/blank-inheritance-ch1-v2.md §4 (Show, Never Tell) and §5 (Mystery Ledger #8), and design/induction.md (the assembly step). ideas/story/blank-inheritance-v4.md already calls it 'the emergency protocol' and marks that as this proposal, with 'if the proposal is vetoed, cut the protocol'. The line about brothers is literal, not metaphor, and belongs to Hyuck ('second son, killed his brother', v4). Hyuck being alive and the Directorate's test pilot of its worst Frame concepts is canon (LEDGER #28), and Steve plays him in flashbacks (LEDGER #31 item 12). Related: hero-points-vs-berserk, whose premise went with Bleed (cut 2026-09-20) and with item 14.

2026-09-24 (LEDGER #32 item 11; Ingram, Casebook N8) -- still open, to be pinned down much later. "Hyuck absolutely would build something like that, but maybe we develop this idea to only happen with Gen 2. Leave it as an open question to be pinned down much later." Read: Hyuck's emergency protocol would exist, but only with Gen 2 (Gen 1 Frames are Golarion technology with no living core, LEDGER #32 item 7). Her answer keeps the protocol and gives it an owner and a machine; its shape is not decided. One thing to check when it is: the protocol is recited at assembly in Chapter 1 (Mystery Ledger #8), while Gen 2 reaches the field only at the end of Chapter 4. The Gen 2 prototypes are decades old and were mothballed (LEDGER #20), so a protocol written for them could already exist; nobody has said so.

questions.question: The generation ship's shuttle is buried deep under the rock of Kortos, away from the ship's ruin. The exotic fuel the four founders were fetching when they caused First Impact was for it, and they never reached it (LEDGER #32 item 5). What is the shuttle, what did the jungle mitflits mean to do with it (and did they know how dangerous the fuel was), is it still there, and how does Blank Inheritance tie the thread up?
questions.notes:
Raised 2026-09-24 from Ingram's answer to Casebook N3 (LEDGER #32): "I cannot remember the original reasoning, so let's assume that it was fuel for the Shuttle. The players never got to the shuttle which was buried deep under the rock of Kortos away from the original destroyed spaceship. We can leave this as something that we need to tie up eventually." Canon: it exists, it is buried deep under the rock of Kortos away from the generation ship, the fuel was for it, and the four never got to it. Everything else is open. Don't assume the obvious reading (a shuttle to fly home, or to go for help); nobody has said it. Things to check it against when it is decided, none of them decided: the old campaign's Kortos map already marked a 'Shuttle Location' (ideas/story/source-material/the-trouble-with-mitflits/campaign-timeline.md; source, not canon); Blank Inheritance exists partly to close the old campaign's loose ends (LEDGER #30); the Directorate was born to guard the Kortos site (LEDGER #32 item 6); and the campaign's last quarter already needs a way to the mitflit home world (LEDGER #26). Not to be confused with the withdrawn 'deep-buried machine' (bisected-specimen-origin), which was the bisected specimen and does not exist. Replaces jungle-mitflit-fuel-purpose, resolved the same day.

2026-09-24 (LEDGER #34, Casebook N25): Anabala's own ultimate objective is a way home for her people, using mitflit technology. CLAUDE'S NOTE, not a decision: the shuttle is one candidate for that way home, and the search ship under Kurose, which lifts at Chapter 15 in the draft, is another.

questions.question: How has William Charles Baldwin stayed alive for two hundred years? Ingram: "He was insanely rich, that might give him access to ways to stay alive" (LEDGER #32). Looted ship technology, bought magic, a bargain with something, or something else?
questions.notes:
Raised 2026-09-24 (LEDGER #32, 'Still open'). GM-only: that he is alive at all is a secret kept until the right moment (baldwin-reveal). Canon underneath it: he is alive, and his wealth bought it somehow. CLAUDE'S PROPOSAL (LEDGER #32, veto freely): he was on Kortos when First Impact opened the generation ship, with hunters, money and a weapons works on the island, so he was among the first to loot the site; ship technology (medical, repair nanites) keeps him alive, and his mitflit slaves, fascinated by that technology, keep it running. Alternatives named in the same entry: bought magic, or a bargain. Things to check it against, none decided: Sap is canon as the generation ship's stock for its repair nanites (LEDGER #32 item 9), so a body kept going by repair nanites sits close to the Watcher's own feedstock; and his file notes that if he runs on ship technology, the Watcher may already be able to see through him. The founders' own longevity is a separate thread (LEDGER #8; Hyuck's is answered by LEDGER #41, the Carrying).

2026-09-24 (LEDGER #33): asked again as Casebook N16 and parked. Ingram: "We'll work this out later."

questions.question: When and how is William Charles Baldwin revealed to the players, and to whom first? Ingram: "This would have to be a reveal we keep secret till the right moment" (LEDGER #32).
questions.notes:
Raised 2026-09-24 (LEDGER #32, 'Still open'). GM-only. Canon: he is alive; the reveal is kept secret until the right moment; the original Tuesday group would be his natural enemies if he revealed himself (Ingram: "The original Tuesday group of Rupiah, Shucks, Anabala and Hyuck would be natural enemies of Baldwin if he revealed himself"); and the moment is personal for the players, four of whom played those four. Until then his name, his face and his survival are held back; his organisation can be felt long before he is (ideas/story/bible/characters/william-charles-baldwin.md). CLAUDE'S PROPOSAL, from his file (veto freely): signs build long before, each deniable on its own (impossible weapons in gang hands, missing mitflits from the gathering, a front company called Croglang, a crime lord nobody has ever seen), so that when he steps out the founders, and their players, know him on sight.

2026-09-24 (LEDGER #33): asked again as Casebook N17 and parked. Ingram: "We'll work this out later."

questions.question: What is the stray, and what does it become? Plainly: a small, broken-off piece of the Watcher (v4 §6) that follows one PC home, waiting to be fed. Ingram calls it "a less developed concept" and leaves it open to be solved later (LEDGER #32 item 13).
questions.notes:
Raised 2026-09-24 from Ingram's answer to Casebook N11 (when the stray's second nature, the microphone, is revealed): "You are being mysterious again. The stray, by which you mean 'The Watcher' right? Or some broken off aspect of The Watcher? This is a less developed concept, so let's leave that an open question to be solved later." Stated plainly, as she asked: the stray is a small, broken-off piece of the Watcher (v4 §6). What exists already, all of it drafted rather than decided: it comes through a lab spill and follows one PC home, patiently, the way the first fragment followed Manako; the player names it; it is a pet and a microphone at once (ideas/story/dossier-observer.md, 'Where it appears'); and in the v4 bible it can become the demonstration that breaks Manako's faith, a piece of the same swarm raised by somebody else. Open: when (or whether) its second nature is revealed, what it becomes if raised kindly, and whether it can ever speak. In GM-facing prose, name it plainly as a piece of the Watcher: 'You are being mysterious again' was her objection to the Casebook calling it only 'the stray'.

2026-09-27 (LEDGER #42): KEPT, as a possibility. Ingram: "Keep it, I think it's an interesting idea and possibility, the players encounter part of The Watcher and then they end up befriending it or it becomes like a mascot, but in fact it's a piece of the thing threatening the whole city. It's a fun idea, we'll have to see if we can make it work." Still open: whether it works at the table, and the details. Claude's proposal for its origin: after a fight in Chapter 5, the one crumb that doesn't drain home.

questions.question: Pippa may choose to keep playing Anabala in the new campaign, as one of the students (LEDGER #32 item 14). Does she, and if so, how does Anabala come to be one of the six?
questions.notes:
Raised 2026-09-24 from Ingram's answer to Casebook N12: "Anabala must be there for it to happen. Anabala may even be one of the 'students' because Pippa may choose to continue playing as Anabala in the new adventure. We can solve this later in the adventure and leave it open for now, but Anabala could be there at the right time and place easily enough." Canon: Anabala must be present for Abraxas to emerge (item 14). Open: whether Pippa plays her as a student. Pippa already plays her in flashbacks (LEDGER #31 item 12). Things this would touch, none of them decided: (1) Abraxas's emergence would happen to a player character, and nothing in this campaign takes a character away from their player (LEDGER #31 item 14), so that version needs working out with Pippa first; (2) the six carry 'the right stuff' by coincidence (LEDGER #31 item 10), but a mitflit carries it natively, and Anabala built Gen 2 (LEDGER #32 item 7); (3) she knows things the rest of the table must not learn early: Frame Sickness (LEDGER #23), the mitflits' whole origin (LEDGER #15), and Abraxas, GM-only and unmentioned for a long time (LEDGER #31 item 20); (4) the six kids are the players' own creative work, and the draft roster in data/characters/kids/ is unconfirmed, so nothing here decides who the six are.

2026-09-24 (LEDGER #33; Ingram, Casebook N23): "Abraxes could emerge from Anabala, but Anabala is still a character that Pippa can play. Not an issue to worry too much about." So item (1) above is settled: the emergence does not take the character from her player. Abraxas comes out; Anabala stays Pippa's. Still open: whether Pippa chooses to play her as a student, how Anabala comes to be one of the six, and items (2) to (4). CLAUDE'S PROPOSAL for what the emergence costs (veto freely): she lived through the ages because of Abraxas, so without the demon she may begin to age, or weaken; a price that is Anabala's and Pippa's to pay or refuse.

questions.question: Whose machine does Bobbin sit in? The sit-in (a pacifist mitflit Elder entering a Frame so it cannot be used, and cannot be extracted without killing him) must not take a player's machine away from them (LEDGER #31 item 14), and LEDGER #32 leaves the answer open (item 17).
questions.notes:
Raised 2026-09-24 from Casebook N15, which Ingram left open: "Let's leave that as an open question to resolve later." The problem as the Casebook put it: the sit-in now sits awkwardly with 'nothing takes control away from a player'; if he sits in a PC's own Frame, a player loses their machine to an NPC. CLAUDE'S PROPOSAL from the Casebook, NOT adopted: he occupies something the city needs instead (a combat-corps Frame, or the search ship's own seat, so it can never be flown as a weapon), which keeps the discomfort without taking anything from a player. LEDGER #32 adds a second constraint: Gen 1 Frames are Golarion technology with no living core (item 7), so if he sits in a Gen 1, 'the Directorate cannot extract them without killing them' (ideas/story/blank-inheritance-v4.md §9) needs a reason other than a core; if he sits in a Gen 2, the answer bears on arc-mitflit-frame-core-link (ideas/story/bible/species/mitflits.md). The bible's own instruction stands either way: do not resolve the discomfort quickly.

2026-09-24 (LEDGER #34, Casebook D13): the Gen 2 core is biomechanical mitflit technology, not a living mitflit, and wild mitflits are uncomfortable around Gen 2 Frames. CLAUDE'S PROPOSAL: if Bobbin sits in a Gen 2, the discomfort is part of his price for the strike, which fits the bible's instruction not to resolve it quickly. Whose machine is still open.

questions.question: A Gen 2 Frame's living core makes a seat shaped to its pilot's true form (LEDGER #5, Gen 2 only since LEDGER #32). In this campaign a disguised PC's reveal belongs to the player, always (design/induction.md §2). How do the two meet when a disguised PC climbs into a Gen 2 Frame: who can see the seat's shape, and can it give away something the player hasn't chosen to reveal?
questions.notes: Raised 2026-09-24 by Claude while filing LEDGER #32; an open question, not a decision. The two facts: (1) the core forms a seat for whoever can link with it, shaped to the pilot's true form, and when a pilot dies the Frame holds that shape in the hangar until it re-forms (LEDGER #5; ideas/story/blank-inheritance-v4.md, 'The cavity conforms'); since #32 this is Gen 2 only, because Gen 1 Frames have no core. (2) Every character presents as human, elf, halfling or similar at the start, and anything else is disguised; and 'The reveal belongs to the player, always. Not to the GM, not to the induction system, not to a skill check somebody else rolls. The system may know; the table finds out when the player decides' (design/induction.md §2). design/induction.md §2 already names the meeting as a scene: 'A character in a borrowed shape climbing into a hollow moulded to their real one is a scene that writes itself, and it is available the first time they sit in a Frame.' Since #32 that is the first time they sit in a Gen 2, at the end of Chapter 4 at the earliest (LEDGER #31 item 13), and that line wants updating to say so. Until this is decided, don't write a Gen 2 cockpit scene with a disguised pilot in it.
questions.resolution: RESOLVED 2026-09-24 (LEDGER #33; Ingram, Casebook N19): "When they enter the machine they find it uncomfortable to do so except in their true form." So a disguised pilot can climb into a Gen 2 and fly it; it is uncomfortable unless they are in their true form. Nothing forces a reveal, and the reveal stays the player's (design/induction.md §2). The natural reading: the seat is shaped to the true body, so a borrowed shape does not fit it. CLAUDE'S FILL-INS (LEDGER #33, veto freely): (1) the v4 bible has a Gen 2 cavity keep its current pilot's shape even when the cockpit is empty ('The cavity conforms'), so a hangar crew could see a hollow shaped to a disguised pilot's true body; the induction rule already covers it ('The system may know; the table finds out when the player decides'): the crew may know, and the GM never describes the hollow's shape to the table until the player reveals. (2) The discomfort is not Frame Sickness (LEDGER #23), which is the sync problem any pilot has in a Gen 2 new to them, disguised or not; keep the two apart. Open, not decided: whether the discomfort ever has a mechanical cost. If it does, it must raise risk in a specific moment and never shrink the pilot's options (design/campaign-arc.md, 'penalties cost risk, never choice').

questions.question: Was Manako arrested, though not imprisoned, as part of the court proceeding over Hori's shooting of the Envoy? Ingram: "Manako may have even been arrested but not imprisoned as part of this, but maybe not" (LEDGER #33).
questions.notes:
Raised 2026-09-24 from Ingram's answer to Casebook N22 (LEDGER #33). Canon around it: Hori learned Aoi's name at a complex court proceeding to decide whether the killing was lawful; on the day he was dealing with a local disturbance, alone, with no backup, and it escalated; the circle scattered from the street, Manako with it (LEDGER #32 item 15). CHECKED, NOT A CONTRADICTION: if he was arrested, it was by the police, as a man at a public disturbance, before Cicada existed, and he was released without charge. That does not identify him as Cicada's founder, and the Directorate has never connected the two, so LEDGER #17 stands. KNOCK-ONS IF IT HAPPENED: (1) Hori may have seen him, or heard his name, at the proceeding (ideas/story/bible/characters/hori.md, open question 4); (2) a fifteen-year-old police record with his name in it exists, which the players can find for themselves; no NPC may point them at it (ideas/story/dossier-cicada.md §13.5).

2026-09-24 (LEDGER #34): Ingram, on this: "Manako could be known to the Directorate and that wouldn't be the worst thing in the world because they can't locate them and they don't know them or understand them." So whether he was arrested no longer matters to LEDGER #17 either way. It stays open as a detail to decide when it is useful.

2026-09-24 (LEDGER #35): the police and the Directorate distrust each other, and what happens with the police doesn't reach the Directorate. So an arrest, if there was one, sits in police records only; the Directorate's whole knowledge of the Envoy incident is its official line, that a cultist was killed during a confrontation in which someone magically summoned a monster.

questions.question: Is a small part of Mother in every Gen 2 Frame, the 'cerebral glue' that makes the technology work? Ingram: "Maybe a small part of 'Mother' ends up in every Gen 2 mech, maybe that's the cerebral glue needed to get the tech to work, but the end result is that these mechs aren't usable by just anyone" (LEDGER #34).
questions.notes: Raised 2026-09-24 from Ingram's answer to Casebook D13 (LEDGER #34). CANON around it: the Gen 2 core is biomechanical mitflit technology, robotic parts that are living flesh melded with technology, not a living mitflit; wild mitflits are uncomfortable around Gen 2 Frames, and mitflits don't instantly understand where Gen 2 comes from; the result is that these mechs aren't usable by just anyone. Gen 2 is built from the original ship's technology, the generation ship at Kortos (LEDGER #20, #34), and Mother was that ship's mind, perhaps still alive in the museum fragment (LEDGER #32 item 3). CLAUDE'S PROPOSALS if it is adopted (veto freely): Anabala took the pieces from the generation ship's reasoning core under the restricted access she bargained for (LEDGER #34, N25), and the museum fragment is one more piece nobody else understands; it would explain why the Watcher's children are drawn hard to Gen 2 (ideas/story/dossier-observer.md, the G3 generation), since each one carries a piece of the mind the Watcher used to report to; and it bears on Mother's voice (Casebook N21) and on mother-and-the-watcher. Don't write it as settled anywhere. Tone guardrail (2026-09-25): this echoes the mother-in-the-machine of the Evangelion research shelf. Take structure from it if useful, never its register (design/research/evangelion/tone-guardrail.md).

questions.question: The founding charter's painted-over paragraph: is it interesting, is it logical, and what should change? Ingram: "I think we need to rethink this whole concept. The founding charter, is it interesting? Is it logical? What should we change about it?" (LEDGER #36).
questions.notes: Raised 2026-09-25 (LEDGER #36). Ingram on the repo's current answer (mystery-ledger-5; dossier-the-directorate.md section 2.2): "it belongs to much older generated ideas and notes that don't really feel sane any more." WHERE IT IS PLANTED: Intake Medicals (the lobby, with a check), Assembly (framed above the platform) and School Period Two (the civics class, where the Advocate has asked to see it and been refused), plus mystery-ledger-5, dossier-the-directorate §2.2 and §8, and the Casebook's Chapter 13 (the deepest vault). WHY THE CURRENT ANSWER FAILS (Claude's analysis): it was written about 195 years ago, before any Frame existed and before the prophecy named Kurose, so it can't foresee child pilots; its authors are alive and on the base, so 'nobody alive has read it' can't hold; the party are volunteers of any age, not conscripted children; and a painted-over paragraph framed in a lobby advertises a secret rather than keeping one. OPTIONS: cut the mystery (the charter becomes plain scenery); or replace what's under the bar with something on today's spine. The strongest candidate is the founders' own account of First Impact, painted out once to keep the heroes clean. It ties the old campaign, the sanitised portraits and the Watcher's origin together, and since the founders are alive, the party can simply ask them.
questions.resolution: Resolved 2026-09-27 (Ingram, LEDGER #41): cut. "Cut it, the charter is a useful document and good lore, but publicly censoring part of it is odd - a secret that is flaunted, hints of 1984 and it makes the Directorate seem evil instead of just very secretive." The charter stays, with nothing painted out, and the old answer is withdrawn everywhere. Claude's proposal for the plant it leaves: the charter's four signatures (Shucks's old hand, which Rand writes in; HYUCK in capitals; Anabala's mitflit script), in Intake Medicals' the-charter check. The Transparency Advocate's refusal is now the inventory of the deep storage vaults (LEDGER #40).

questions.question: Do damaged machines still lose actions under lockstep? The retired two-scale design capped a Degraded Frame or vehicle at 2 actions, a Critical one at 1, and a Hulked one at 0. design/ux-doctrine.md §3 still builds on that, and config.json now records it, but nobody has re-confirmed it since Frames became PC-grade sheets that amplify the pilot.
questions.notes: Raised 2026-09-25 in the stale-material cull, when the only document that defined the caps (design/scale-and-chassis.md §8) was deleted. The rule fits 'penalties cost risk, never choice' (campaign-arc.md): the cap is a dynamic, recoverable state, not a permanent tax. Kept in config.json#frameEconomy.damageStateEffects until Ingram decides.
